title: Read It Again, More Slowly: A Scripture-Prayer Practice for One Phrase
subtitle: Lectio divina invites Christians to read a short passage more than once, attend to what catches their attention and answer in prayer—without forcing a revelation or a particular feeling.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table with an open Bible, a notebook and mugs of tea, taking a quiet moment to read together.

body: A way of reading, not a test

Lectio divina is a Christian practice of reading Scripture slowly and prayerfully. The Latin phrase is often translated as “divine reading”; the Anglican Communion describes it as contemplative Bible reading and prayer [1]. Rather than moving quickly to explain a passage, the reader returns to it, listens for a word or phrase that stands out, reflects, and responds. Versions vary, but many follow four movements: reading, meditation, contemplation and prayer [2]. These are invitations, not boxes to tick perfectly.

The practice can be done alone or with other people, and it does not require a particular setting, religious training or a long stretch of time. A short passage and a few attentive minutes are enough to begin. The aim is not to extract a clever interpretation or produce a spiritual experience on demand. For Christians, it is a way of meeting Scripture as part of prayer.
Why return to the same lines?

A first reading often gives us the broad outline: who is speaking, what happens, where the scene turns. A second, slower reading makes room for a detail to register—a repeated word, a surprising response, a moment of silence or a phrase that feels difficult. Returning to the text is not a way to make every line carry a secret message. It is a way to give attention time to settle before deciding what a passage means.

That distinction matters. A phrase may feel comforting, puzzling, even irritating. The practice does not require treating any reaction as a command or a prediction. Instead, you can notice what arose and ask a modest question: What might this passage be showing me about God, another person, or the way I am living? An honest “I don’t know” is a real response, not a failure.
Choose a passage with room to pause

Pick a short section—perhaps a few verses from a Gospel story, a psalm, or another passage you already know. A complete scene can help because it gives the words some context; a single striking verse may also work. If you are new to the practice, choose a passage that interests you rather than one you feel obliged to understand. Read it in a translation you can follow, and keep the surrounding verses available if a line seems unclear.

Find a comfortable place where you can give the text a little attention. You may read silently, aloud, or take turns with a friend. There is no special breathing technique and no need to empty your mind. If other thoughts arrive, you can acknowledge them and return to the words. If a passage raises a hard question, you do not have to resolve it in the moment; keeping the question visible can be more faithful than rushing toward an answer.

Try a flexible practice of about ten minutes. First, read the passage once at an ordinary pace to hear the whole scene. Pause briefly. Read it again more slowly, noticing any words, images or turns in the story that draw your attention. You can read it a third time if useful, but repetition is an invitation, not a rule. The Anglican Communion and Catholic resources describe this kind of movement from reading toward reflection, prayer and quiet [1][2].

Next, stay with one word or phrase. Ask what you notice about it and what, if anything, it brings to mind in your life. Keep the passage in view: reflection is not permission to detach a line from its context or make it say whatever you wish. Then respond in a way that fits your faith—silently, in a few written lines, or in prayer. You might offer gratitude, ask for help, name a question or say nothing. Finish with a short quiet pause. There is no required emotional result.
Let prayer be plain and specific

A response does not need to sound polished. If a passage brings a person or situation to mind, you might pray for them by name. If it surfaces a concern about your own choices, you could ask for clarity or courage, without assuming that the text has already supplied a simple answer. A notebook can hold a phrase, a question or a brief response; it need not become a record of spiritual progress.

In a group, keep the invitation open. Each person can share a word or thought, pass, or listen without explaining themselves. One person’s response does not have to become the group’s interpretation. The USCCB describes lectio divina in parish and small-group settings as well as personal prayer [2], but a shared setting still benefits from ordinary care: listen without correcting, do not press for disclosure, and allow differing responses to remain different.

Lectio divina comes from Christian prayer, and that context is central rather than incidental. Someone outside the Christian tradition may find value in reading a short text slowly, but using that structure with another kind of writing is an adaptation, not the same religious practice. Naming the difference makes room for curiosity without flattening the meaning it holds for Christians.

A classroom essay on a secular adaptation discusses both the attention such reading can bring to a person’s responses and possible difficulties, including limited time, engagement and the way participants may perceive its religious character [3]. That is a discussion of a teaching context, not evidence that lectio divina improves health. This practice is not therapy or medical care, and it cannot promise relief, certainty or a particular feeling. If a passage causes distress or brings up something that needs support, it is reasonable to stop and turn to a trusted person or qualified professional.
Try it with the road to Emmaus

For a first reading, you could choose Luke 24:28–32, part of the story in which two disciples recognize Jesus after walking and sharing a meal. Read the passage once for the scene, then again for a detail that stays with you: the invitation to remain, the breaking of bread, or the disciples’ reflection on their hearts. Ask what that detail raises for you, without insisting it must match anyone else’s answer. If you are reading with a friend, each of you can share a sentence or pass. End by sitting quietly for a moment, then close the Bible and leave any unresolved question as a question.
